verdict.reasoning: Seven of eleven dispatches returned nothing because the query never reached its backend, and each specialist was explicit that this is a transport failure rather than an empty result set, explicitly refusing to read the emptiness as a clean bill of health [tr_e66eea973aa7, tr_8e06eccc4879, tr_bf905e3b47c4, tr_e81ca40ccc7b]. Choosing a fault class requires precisely the missing discriminators: a freeze is told from a partition by whether the culprit logs anything, a disk fill from a bad config by what it writes, exhaustion from latency by whether it died or waited. None is available. The change evidence is consistent and negative across all four services — no image bump, no config mutation, no rollout to an existing workload, no human actor, only a single atomic first creation seven minutes before onset [tr_0968b4b0cc91, tr_a5b95ee9dcf7, tr_789300c8ad7c]. This excludes a regression-style bad_deploy and makes rollback unavailable, since no prior revision exists for any service. It does not supply a mechanism. The next step is restoring the investigator's DNS path to the observe namespace and re-running the selectors, which specialists confirmed were well-formed and never evaluated.
verdict.root_cause: Not established. Every observability dispatch failed in the tooling transport path — Prometheus, Loki and Jaeger hostnames all failed DNS resolution from the querying environment, so no metric, log or trace signal was obtained for any of the four services. The only substantive evidence is the change log: nginx-web-server, compose-post-service, home-timeline-service and user-timeline-service were each stood up for the first time at 17:16:04–17:16:05 by platform-automation, with ConfigMap, Service and container created together and no prior revision of any of them in the 24-hour window. That establishes the whole stack is seven minutes old at onset — so whatever is failing has been failing since first start rather than regressing — but it does not identify which service is at fault or by what mechanism. nginx-web-server is named only as the edge where failure was observed, not as a demonstrated culprit.

alternatives.why_not: Plausible on timing and on these being first creations, but wholly unevidenced: no one read the ConfigMap contents, and specialists ruled out config mutation without testing whether the created values are correct [tr_a5b95ee9dcf7]. Picking this service over the other three would be arbitrary, and there is no prior value to revert to.
alternatives.root_cause: One of the four services was stood up with an originally wrong value in its freshly created ConfigMap or Service — wrong address, port or credential — so it has never served correctly.

alternatives.why_not: The only resolution failures observed are on the investigation host against observe-namespace endpoints, and a specialist explicitly ruled out treating that as the incident's own DNS fault surfacing in a service dependency chain [tr_1ceb73156868]. A partition verdict requires the culprit's own log complaining it cannot reach anything, and no service log was retrieved at all.
alternatives.root_cause: Cluster DNS is degraded, so social-network services cannot resolve their dependencies — the same resolution fault that blocked every observability query.

open_questions: Which of the four services is actually failing — no trace, metric or log evidence implicates or exonerates any of them [tr_bf905e3b47c4].
Did the containers created at 17:16:04 reach a healthy running state or fail at startup? This needs kube events or restart counts, since the log path is unusable [tr_415f12bc7d74].

Is the DNS failure confined to the investigation tooling, or is cluster DNS degraded in a way that would also break service-to-service resolution inside social-network? The client-side judgement [tr_1ceb73156868] rests on the host being an observability endpoint, not on any test of in-cluster resolution.

draft.title: Edge failure at nginx-web-server with no usable observability signal

sections.body:
The page came from nginx-web-server. Four services were in the declared blast radius: nginx-web-server at the edge, plus compose-post-service, home-timeline-service and user-timeline-service behind it. Severity was called critical. Three of the edges between those services had never been measured, so there was no prior shape of normal traffic to compare against.

That is, honestly, everything that was visible. Read the rest of this record as an account of an investigation that did not get off the ground, and of which doors were tried.
sections.heading: What was visible at the start

sections.body:
The first dispatch was a metric baseline on nginx-web-server — an error-ratio over span-derived call counts, incident window against the half hour before it. It came back empty. The important detail, and the one that cost the most time to internalise, is that it was empty because the request never left the querying environment: the Prometheus hostname could not be resolved. No connection was attempted, no query was evaluated.

So there is no 5xx rate, no latency figure, no per-upstream or per-route breakdown for the edge, for either window.
sections.heading: First moves: metrics at the edge

sections.body:
The tempting reading was that nginx-web-server had zero 5xx in the window — a flat edge, with the problem necessarily downstream. That reading is wrong. An errored request and a successful request returning no series look alike from a distance and mean opposite things. Nothing here says anything about nginx's error behaviour in either direction.

Two adjacent dead ends, both tried and both worthless: rewriting the PromQL (the expression was never evaluated, so its correctness was never tested) and adjusting the window or baseline range (those parameters rode along in a request that never arrived). Also not supportable: the conclusion that Prometheus had stopped scraping span metrics for the service. The backend was never contacted; its state is untested.
sections.heading: Dead end: reading the empty metric result as a finding

sections.body:
Logs for nginx-web-server, scoped to the social-network namespace with a pod selector over the full onset window, failed identically: the Loki hostname did not resolve. The same for compose-post-service, home-timeline-service and user-timeline-service. The trace query against the Jaeger endpoint failed the same way.

The trace failure hurt most. That query was the one that would have named which downstream hop carried ERROR status or dominated latency. No spans came back, so none of the three downstream services is implicated and none is exonerated.

By the time metrics were tried again — on compose-post-service — the metrics path had been marked unavailable after three consecutive failures and was not retried at all. Reformulating that query would not have helped.
sections.heading: Logs, traces — same wall

sections.body:
At one point the name-resolution errors looked like the answer — the incident surfacing in the dependency chain. It does not hold up on the evidence collected. The names that failed to resolve are observability backend hosts, failing on the querying client's side, appearing in tool transport errors rather than in any log line emitted by a workload in social-network. No test of in-cluster service-to-service resolution was ever run.

That said, this is a judgement, not a proof. Whether cluster name resolution is degraded in a way that would also break calls between the four services is genuinely open, and a responder picking this up should test it directly rather than inherit the assumption.
sections.heading: Dead end worth keeping: treating the resolution failures as the incident

sections.body:
Change history returned real data for all four services, and the four stories are identical. Each service has exactly three entries in the whole 24-hour window, all attributed to platform-automation, all clustered within a second or two at roughly T-7m relative to onset: a ConfigMap created, a Service created, and a container workload created for the first time.

Created, not modified. No prior revision of any of the four exists in the window. The whole stack is about seven minutes old when the page fires.

This closes several hypotheses cleanly. There was no image bump or version rollout regressing a previously healthy service — the only container events are first creations. There was no edit to an existing nginx upstream block or to any ConfigMap value — every config object is a creation, not an update. No human operator touched anything; every entry carries the automated actor. No slow drift from earlier in the day accumulated into this; the 24-hour window holds nothing else.

It also kills the obvious remediation. Rolling back is not available for any of the four, because there is no earlier state to roll back to. A rollback here would be a deletion.
sections.heading: The one channel that worked: the change log

sections.body:
No cause established. Confidence low, no fix class identified.

What the change log does buy is a reframe. Because every one of these services was born seven minutes before onset, the failure is not a working thing that broke — it is something that never worked correctly from first start. That changes what a responder should look for: original misconfiguration, a container that never reached a healthy running state, a dependency that was never wired up right. Not a regression.

What it does not buy is attribution. nginx-web-server is where the failure was observed, nothing more. It is not a demonstrated culprit, and the three downstream services are equally unexamined.
sections.heading: Where this landed

sections.body:
First, fix the observability transport. Every modality failed in the same place for the same reason, and until a query from the investigating environment can actually reach Prometheus, Loki or Jaeger, no amount of query tuning produces anything. The selectors and windows used here were sound in shape and can be reused verbatim once access is restored.

Second, go around the broken log path. The question of whether those containers created at T-7m reached a healthy running state or died at startup is answerable from kube events and container restart counts, neither of which depends on the log store.

Third, test in-cluster name resolution directly from inside social-network. That settles whether the resolution trouble is confined to the tooling or is a cluster-wide condition that would also explain service-to-service failures — and if it is the latter, the picture changes substantially.
sections.heading: What to try next

proposal.risk: The risk of abstaining is that a genuinely broken service stays broken for longer while DNS or event access is repaired; the four services have been failing since first start seven minutes before onset, so no further degradation is accumulating from a previously-working state. The risk of NOT abstaining is larger and concrete: the three plausible actions each fail their preconditions. rollback_image and revert_config have no prior revision or prior config to return to for any of these four services — all recorded events are first creations by platform-automation [tr_0968b4b0cc91, tr_a5b95ee9dcf7, tr_0a7a4390ab64, tr_789300c8ad7c] — so a rollback would amount to deleting a service that may be the only working part of the stack. restart_service requires evidence pointing at process state, and there is none: no trace, metric or log signal implicates or exonerates any of the four [tr_bf905e3b47c4, tr_415f12bc7d74, tr_e81ca40ccc7b]. Restarting a service picked without evidence is a one-in-four guess, is irreversible, discards cache, and would muddy the startup-failure question that kube events still have to answer.
proposal._note: Also recorded: scale_service, reconnect_service, restore_store and free_storage are listed UNAVAILABLE in the brief, so even if the mechanism were shown to be a missing network attachment or a poisoned store, this system could not act on it — a further reason the honest output here is an abstention rather than a substitute action.
proposal.if_wrong: This abstention is wrong if someone produces evidence meeting an action's precondition — e.g. kube events or restart counts showing one of the four containers in CrashLoopBackOff or repeatedly restarting since 17:16:04, which would point at process state and justify restart_service on that specific service. It is also wrong if change history outside the 24-hour window shows a prior image tag or prior ConfigMap for one of these services, which would make rollback_image or revert_config eligible. Note separately: with Prometheus, Loki and Jaeger all unreachable from this vantage point [tr_e66eea973aa7, tr_8e06eccc4879, tr_bf905e3b47c4], the effect of ANY remediation taken now could not be observed through metrics, logs or traces — an unverifiable action is a second reason to hold.
proposal.blast_radius: Nobody. No service is touched and no caller sees a change. For contrast, had an action been proposed: a restart or rollback of compose-post-service, home-timeline-service or user-timeline-service would be seen as a connection reset by nginx-web-server, which is the inbound edge to all three and the alerted edge of this incident; an action on nginx-web-server itself would be seen by every external caller of the social-network namespace, since it is the edge.
proposal.expected_effect: No action proposed, so no effect is expected. Nothing in the system state should change as a result of this proposal. The useful next step is not a remediation at all: restore the investigation host's DNS resolution for prometheus-server.observe.svc.cluster.local, loki.observe.svc.cluster.local and jaeger-out.observe.svc.cluster.local, or obtain kube events and container restart counts for the four workloads out-of-band, so that a culprit can be named before anything is touched.
